messages.subject: Re: Dotplot, position="stack"
messages.body_plain:
I decided to change it from using position="stack" to stackgroups=TRUE.
- This makes it clear that it's not using the normal position adjustment methods.
- Getting it to work on the y-axis is simple.
- It prints a message when you try to use position="stack", saying that you probably want to use stackgroups=TRUE instead.
- The code is cleaner. Using position="stack" was messy and circumvented some normal behavior.

I've attached a bunch of examples. The last two show how to plot two groups along a center line, and they don't require the new stackgroups parameter -- they can be done without the new modifications.

set.seed(113)
data <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100),
                   y = rnorm(100),
                   group = c(rep("A", 40), rep("B", 60)))

# histodot, no stackgroups
ggplot(data, aes(x=x, fill=group)) +

  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.2, method="histodot", alpha=0.5)

# histodot with stackgroups
ggplot(data, aes(x=x, fill=group)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.2, method="histodot", stackgroups=TRUE, alpha=0.5)

# dotdensity with bins aligned across groups (binpositions="all"), no stackgroups
ggplot(data, aes(x=x, fill=group)) +

  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.2, binpositions="all", alpha=0.5)

# dotdensity with bins aligned across groups (binpositions="all"), and stackgroups
ggplot(data, aes(x=x, fill=group)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.2, binpositions="all", stackgroups=TRUE, alpha=0.5)

# Vertical, no stackgroups
ggplot(aes(x=1, y=x, fill=group), data=data) +
  geom_dotplot(binaxis="y", binwidth=.2, method="histodot", alpha=0.5)

# Vertical, with stackgroups
ggplot(aes(x=1, y=x, fill=group), data=data) +
  geom_dotplot(binaxis="y", binwidth=.2, method="histodot", stackgroups=TRUE,
               alpha=0.5)

# stackgroups with stackdir="center"
ggplot(aes(x=x, fill=group), data=data) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.2, method="histodot", stackgroups=TRUE, stackdir="center")

# stackgroups with stackdir="center", vertical
ggplot(aes(x=1, y=x, fill=group), data=data) +
  geom_dotplot(binaxis="y", binwidth=.2, method="histodot",
               stackgroups=TRUE, stackdir="center")

# Stacking along centerline (doesn't require stackgroups!)
ggplot(aes(x=x, fill=group), data=data) +
  geom_dotplot(data = subset(data, group=="A"), binwidth=.2,
               method="histodot", stackdir="up") +
  geom_dotplot(data = subset(data, group=="B"), binwidth=.2,
               method="histodot", stackdir="down")

# Stacking along centerline, vertical  (doesn't require stackgroups!)
ggplot(aes(x=1, y=x, fill=group), data=data) +
  geom_dotplot(data = subset(data, group=="A"), binaxis="y", binwidth=.2,
               method="histodot", stackdir="up") +
  geom_dotplot(data = subset(data, group=="B"), binaxis="y", binwidth=.2,
               method="histodot", stackdir="down")

-Winston

- position="stack" should be the default, and the current behaviour when aligning from the x or y axis should be what happens when position="identity"

So maybe you could consider making an exception to map colour to the fill+stroke of your circles when the default shape is used. If, at some point, other shapes become available, then this might be reconsidered.

Thanks again for your hard work, I love dotplots ;)

messages.body_plain:
# devtools

The aim of `devtools` is to make your life as a package developer
easier by providing R functions that simplify many common tasks.
Devtools is opinionated about how to do package development, and
requires that you use `roxygen2` for documentation and `testthat` for
testing. Future version will relax these opinions - patches are
welcome! You can track (and contribute to) development of `devtools`
at https://github.com/hadley/devtools.

For discussion related to package development with devtools see the
[rdevtools](http://groups.google.com/group/rdevtools) mailing list.

devtools 0.6
------------

NEW FEATURES

* `test` function takes `filter` argument which allows you to restrict which
  tests are to be run

* `check` runs with example timings, as is done on CRAN. Run with new param
  `cleanup = F` to access the timings.

* `missing_s3` function to help figure out if you've forgotten to export any
  s3 methods

* `check_cran` downloads and checks a CRAN package - this is useful to run as
  part of the testing process of your package if you want to check the
  dependencies of your package

* `strict` mode for `run_examples` which runs each example in a clean
  environment. This is much slower than the default (running in the current
  environment), but ensures that each example works standalone.

* `dev_mode` now updates prompt to indicate that it's active (Thanks to Kohske
  Takahashi)

* new `source_url` function for sourcing script on a remote server via
  protocols other than http (e.g. https or ftp). (Thanks to Kohske Takahashi)

* new `source_gist` function to source R code stored in a github gist. (Thanks
  to Kohske Takahashi)

* `load_all` now also loads all package dependencies (including suggestions) -
  this works around some bugs in the way that devtools attaches the
  development environment into the search path in a way that fails to recreate
  what happens normally during package loading.

INSTALLATION

* remote installation will ensure the configure file is executable.

* all external package installation functions are vectorised so you can
  install multiple packages at time

* new `install_gitorious` function install packages in gitorious repos.

* new `install_url` function for installing package from an arbitrary url

* include `install_version` function from Jeremy Stephens for installing a
  specific version of a CRAN package from the archive.

BETTER WINDOWS BEHAVIOUR

* better check for OS type (thanks to Brian Ripley)

* better default paths for 64-bit R on windows (Fixes #35)

* check to see if Rtools is already available before trying to mess with the
  paths. (Fixes #55)

BUG FIXES

* if an error occurs when calling loading R files, the cache will be
  automatically cleared so that all files are loaded again next time you try
  (Fixes #55)

* functions that run R now do so with `R_LIBS` set to the current
  `.libPaths()` - this will ensure that checking uses the development library
  if you are in development mode. `R_ENVIRON_USER` is set to an empty file to
  avoid your existing settings overriding this.

* `load_data` (called by `load_all`) will also load data defined in R files in
  the data directory. (Fixes #45)

* `dev_mode` performs some basic tests to make sure you're not setting your
  development library to a directory that's not already an R library. (Fixes
  #25)

messages.subject: Idea for new theming system
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm starting to think about a theming system that's easier to
customise, where you can easily specify the properties of all text
elements, all axis elements etc.  Here's what I've come up with so
far:

theme <- list()

theme$text <- list(size = 12, family = "Helvetica", lineheight = 0.9,
  vjust = 1, hjust = 0.5, angle = 0)
theme$title <- list(face = "bold")

theme$axis.text <- list(size = 10, colour = "grey50")
theme$axis.text.y <- list(angle = 0)
theme$axis.ticks <- list(colour = "grey50")
theme$axis.title <- list(vjust = 0.5)
theme$axis.title.y <- list(angle = 90)

theme$background <- list(fill = "white", colour = NA)

theme$legend.background <- list(colour = "white")
theme$legend.key <- list(fill = "grey95", colour = "white")
theme$legend.text <- list(size = 10)
theme$legend.tite <- list()

theme$strip.text <- list(size = 10)
theme$strip.text.y <- list(angle = -90)
theme$strip.background <- list(fill = "grey80", colour = NA)

theme$panel.background <- list(fill = "grey80", colour = NA)

theme$plot.title <- list(size = 14)

# Rename all components into alphabetical order
names(theme) <- sapply(strsplit(names(theme), ".", fixed = T), function(x) {
  paste(sort(x), collapse = ".")
})

theme_find <- function(component) {
  pieces <- sort(strsplit(component, ".", fixed = TRUE)[[1]])

  combs <- expand.grid(rep(list(c(T, F)), length(pieces)),
    KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE)
  combs <- unrowname(combs[order(rowSums(combs))[-1], ])
  labels <- apply(combs, 1, function(x) paste(pieces[x], collapse = "."))

  elements <- theme[intersect(labels, names(theme))]
  Reduce(modifyList, elements)
}

theme_find("text.x.axis")
theme_find("text.y.axis")
theme_find("text.x.strip")
theme_find("text.y.strip")

Any thoughts or comments would be greatly appreciated.

Hadley

messages.subject: Visual test system
messages.body_plain:
Hi all -

I've been working on a visual testing system for ggplot2. The basic idea is that you run the visual tests and store the resulting images in the git repo; then at any later time you can re-run the tests and it will (A) tell you if anything changed, and (B) visually display the changes. I started writing it up here:
https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/wiki/Visual-test-system

Hopefully it'll reduce the number of bugs that enter the ggplot2 codebase, by helping us catch them right away.

Here are some web pages that are automatically generated by the system. These are probably more exciting to look at than the wiki page above.
This one shows the results from a test run:
http://stdout.org/~winston/visual_test/html/aspect-ratio/

This one compares the current test results to those from a previous commit in the repo:
http://stdout.org/~winston/visual_test/diff/diff/visual_test/aspect-ratio/

Feedback is welcome!
-Winston

I hadn't heard of it before. I looked into how tools::compactPDF actually works, and it appears to use qpdf, which is a command-line utility included with R (at least it is on the Mac distribution of R).

I did some experimentation with qpdf, turning off compression because the output files should be text rather than compressed binary files. The compression results in savings for each file, but I think I ran this on PDF files generated by ggsave:
  qpdf --stream-data=uncompress in.pdf out.pdf
It appears to take off 6KB of the file size for small files and large ones. The small files were scatterplots of mtcars data (15094 --> 8815 bytes), and the large ones were scatterplots of diamonds data (4084909 --> 4078631)

Next I compared the git storage efficiency of raw PDFs vs. those processed with qpdf without compression, vs. those processed through qpdf with compression. I added 67 PDFs from visual tests to new git repositories. I made three new git repositories with the PDFs processed in different ways:
1. raw
2. qpdf --stream-data=uncompress
3. qpdf --stream-data=compress

Then I ran 'git gc --aggressive' to clean up the repo. The final sizes of the .git/ directories were almost the same:
1. raw: 155,861 bytes
2. qpdf, uncompress: 155,642 bytes
3. qpdf, compress: 207,322 bytes

So using qpdf with compression results in a larger repo size. Using qpdf without compression results in a barely smaller repo, and it saves 6KB per file in the working tree. I'm thinking that the modest savings are probably not worth the extra complexity...

-Winston

I know there's a package called graphicsQC by Paul Murrell which might be used for that stuff, but it seemed kind of a heavy-weight solution, and didn't integrate with git as far as I could tell.

I had a thought about how to store the test images. It is of course possible to store them in the master branch. The drawback is that it's impossible to ever remove the test images from the repository. Also, this doesn't record information about the last time someone ran the tests -- if the test images come out unchanged, then there's nothing to commit, and no record of it in the repository.

One alternative is to store the test images in side branches. For example, make a branch off 0.9.0 called 0.9.0-vtest, run the tests, and commit them to that branch. These side branches could be made off any commit, and they would inherently record information about which commit was tested. They could also be deleted from the repository, freeing up space if that ever becomes an issue. The one drawback I can think of is that it could clutter up the branch namespace. It's kind of unorthodox, but it's worth considering.

-Winston

messages.subject: Visual testing, take 2
messages.body_plain:
Based on the discussion about the previous iteration of the visual test system, I've rewritten it, making some major changes. It now has it's own package, 'vtest', and it can be used with any R package, not just ggplot2. The previous feedback was very helpful, so if you have thoughts about the current version, please feel free to share.

Here's a summary of the major changes:
- vtest is now a separate package
- Test results are stored separately from package repo.
- Test results do not have to be stored in a git repo (but they can be, if desired).
- It uses its own database to keep track of test results, instead of relying on git.
- The test images are hashed with MD5 and are renamed to match the MD5 hash. This makes it easy to keep track of changes and to avoid storing duplicate images.

The biggest conceptual change is that it extensively uses hashes to keep track of what has changed, and to avoid duplication.

I've written about it in more depth here: https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/wiki/Visual-test-system
Some of the wiki page is the same as before. Most of the changes are in the Overview and Internals section. In the Internals, I explain the database format and the file storage layout. I also have a section which contains some ideas about distributed testing and storage of test results.

One thing I'm wondering is where to put the test results. Right now, if your repo is in /somepath/ggplot2/, it puts the test results in /somepath/ggplot2-vtest/. It might make more sense to put the test results in ggplot2/visual_test/results/. The visual_test/ directory already exists, because that's where the test scripts are. If the results went there, there would need to be a .gitignore so that the results don't get added to the ggplot2 repo. (The results could be their own repo.)

You can see examples of the test and comparison output pages here:
Test results: http://stdout.org/~winston/ggplot2-vtest/html/
Comparison results: http://stdout.org/~winston/ggplot2-vtest/diff/

The code is here: https://github.com/wch/vtest
It should be installable via: install_github('vtest', 'wch')
But there are a couple things I have to clean up before it's really ready for others to try out, and I need to update the instructions.

Also, I converted most of the existing ggplot2 visual tests to be used in the new system, but there are some tests that don't work, and other tests that need a description which I'm unable to provide since the purpose of the tests isn't always clear to me. I'll probably post again asking for help regarding those tests.

Hopefully we'll soon be able to starting using the visual tests for ggplot2!

-Winston

Hi everyone -

I'm trying to figure out why ggplot2 does stuff at very different speeds on different machines, and I was hoping you could help collect data.

dev.off()
unlink('temp.pdf')  # Remove the temporary file

time  # Print time info

dput(list(ver = R.Version(), time = time))

https://docs.google.com/spreadsheet/viewform?formkey=dDd6b2Q5MG9ic2NoQWRPT3dLT0FyUkE6MQ

I don't know how to collect information about the CPU from within R, so the form also asks you to enter that information. (I don't know that much about the various kinds of CPUs, especially AMD hardware, so if there are any common CPU types that I'm missing, please let me know.)

Thanks!
-Winston

messages.subject: extract legend grob
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I'm trying to update an old example of sharing a common legend between
two graphs [*]. The old trick opts(keep = "legend_box") doesn't work
anymore in v0.9. Instead, I believe one should build the gtable and
work from there. Consider the example below,

library(ggplot2)
dsamp <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 1000), ]

p1 <- qplot(carat, price, data=dsamp, colour=clarity)

tmp <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p1))
legend <- tmp$grobs[[9]]
# grid.draw(legend)

I manually located the legend grob; it could be automated as

which(sapply(tmp$grobs, function(x) x$name) == "guide-box")

but it seems very inelegant. Have I overlooked a better trick?

Thanks,

baptiste

[*] http://code.google.com/p/gridextra/wiki/arrangeGrob
